entities.name: Giovanni da Amelia
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Giovanni d'Amelia (b. c. 1309, Amelia), originally Giovanni di Bartolomeo, emerged as a prominent Italian cardinal during the tumultuous late 14th century, a period defined by the nascent Western Schism and profound ecclesiastical upheaval. Elevated to the cardinalate by Pope Urban VI in 1378, d'Amelia's career spanned a critical juncture where the authority of the Roman pontiff was fiercely contested, and loyalty to the Holy See was fraught with political and personal peril. His trajectory, from a skilled canon lawyer to a cardinal involved in papal intrigue, illuminates the intense power struggles and shifting alliances that characterized the Avignonese Papacy's aftermath and the subsequent schism.

Initially a staunch supporter of Pope Urban VI following the controversial election of 1378, Cardinal d'Amelia was instrumental in the early attempts to consolidate Urban's authority against the Avignon anti-pope Clement VII. He served as a papal legate, undertaking diplomatic missions that sought to secure allegiances for the Roman line. However, the increasingly autocratic and volatile nature of Urban VI, particularly his treatment of the College of Cardinals, sowed dissent among his closest advisors. D'Amelia, along with several other cardinals, became embroiled in a conspiracy to depose Urban VI, culminating in their arrest at Nocera in 1385.

The consequence of d'Amelia's involvement in the plot against Urban VI was swift and brutal. Following torture, he was executed on January 27, 1386, near Genoa, along with five other cardinals, by order of the Pope himself. This shocking act of papal retribution sent ripples across Europe, further deepening the schism by alienating many who might otherwise have supported the Roman pontiff. His execution underscored the extreme measures taken by both sides to assert legitimacy and control during an era when the very fabric of the Catholic Church was rent by division.

His fate illustrates the extreme political and religious turmoil of late medieval Europe.
